concept.title: Types of Cookies
concept.shortdesc: There are several different types of cookies like persistent cookies, session cookies, first-party cookies, third-party cookies, and the supercookie.

conbody.p: Persistent Cookies are stored on your computer for a predetermined period, even after you close your browser. These cookies have an expiration date, which determines how long they remain on your computer, ranging from a few days to several years. They’re often used for:

ul.li: Authentication: Remembering your login information and keeping you logged into your accounts. Many websites use persistent cookies to remember your login details so you don’t have to enter them every time you visit.

Tracking: Recording your browsing habits and preferences over time, building a profile of your interests. This information can be used to personalize your experience on a website or to deliver targeted advertising.

conbody.p: Session Cookies are temporary and are deleted when you close your browser. They exist only during your active browsing session and are essential for many website features to work correctly. They’re typically used for:

ul.li: Session Management: Maintaining the continuity of your browsing session and keeping track of your activity on a website. Session cookies ensure that the website remembers your actions as you navigate from page to page.

Shopping Carts: Remembering the items you’ve added to your shopping cart as you browse an e-commerce website. Without session cookies, your shopping cart would be emptied every time you move to a different page.

conbody.p: First-party Cookies are set by the website you’re visiting directly. These cookies are generally considered safe and are used to enhance your browsing experience on that particular website. They’re commonly used for:

ul.li: Website Functionality: Enabling essential features like shopping carts, user accounts, and personalized content. Many websites rely on first-party cookies to remember your preferences and tailor the content to your interests.

User Preferences: Storing your preferences for a website, such as language selection, region, or theme. These cookies remember your choices so you don’t have to set them again every time you visit the website.

conbody.p: Third-party Cookies: are set by domains other than the website you’re visiting, often through embedded content like advertisements or videos. These cookies are primarily used for tracking your online behavior across multiple websites. Here’s how they work:

ul.li: You visit a website (website A) that contains an ad from an advertising network (website B).
When the ad loads, website B sets a cookie on your computer.
As you browse other websites that also contain ads from website B, the cookie allows website B to track your activity across these different sites.

conbody.p: A third-party cookie collects data about your online behavior and passes it on to advertisers for insightful advertising, enabling them to display targeted ads based on your activities.

p.note: Due to growing privacy concerns, major web browsers are phasing out support for third-party cookies. Some browsers, like Safari and Firefox, already block them by default. However, many websites still rely on third-party cookies, and some companies are exploring alternative tracking methods, such as browser fingerprinting.

conbody.p: Supercookies are a more persistent type of tracking cookie that’s stored outside of your browser’s usual cookie storage. They can be notoriously difficult to remove and have a knack for reappearing even after you’ve deleted your browser cookies. This is because they’re often stored in multiple locations, including Flash Local Shared Objects, HTML5 Web Storage, and other browser plugins. Supercookies raise significant privacy concerns because they can track your browsing activity across multiple websites and devices, making it challenging to maintain your online privacy.
